race_overlay.weather: July in Idaho Springs, Colorado — Late July in Idaho Springs starts warm (65-75F at 7,540 ft) but temperatures plummet as you ascend. Above treeline at 11,500 ft, wind chill can drive effective temperatures below freezing even in July. The summit at 14,130 ft regularly sees temperatures in the 30s-40s F with sustained wind. Snow and sleet are possible at any time of year. The sun is brutally intense above 10,000 ft. Rehearse adaptable layers and race-day kit changes in the final 2 weeks, including rain protection and wet-road braking, and practice stable positioning in crosswinds before Bob Cook Memorial Mt. Blue Sky Hill Climb (formerly Mt. Evans). Use the organizer's current forecast and safety instructions for final choices.
race_overlay.nutrition: Use training to rehearse an eating and drinking plan that matches the ride duration, intensity, and weather. Use the organizer's current resupply plan for final carry decisions.
race_overlay.altitude: Bob Cook Memorial Mt. Blue Sky Hill Climb (formerly Mt. Evans) includes meaningful altitude exposure. Reduced oxygen availability can affect sustainable power, pacing, and recovery. Use a conservative upper-mountain pacing plan, test any travel or acclimatization strategy before the event, and plan layers for changing conditions. Do not begin iron or other supplements without clinician-guided testing. Temperature drop of 30-40F from start to summit — hypothermia is a real risk; 40%+ reduction in oxygen at the summit — breathing is labored even standing still.

pack_summary: This 10-workout pack focuses on VO2max, Race Simulation, and Over Under to prepare you for 27 miles of paved mountain highway to extreme altitude in Idaho Springs, Colorado.
